title: Who Ya Gonna Call? Scam Busters!
author: Carolyn Wells
content:
Mark Seal is very fond of the phrase “Who Ya Gonna Call? Scam Busters!”—he uses it three times in this piece. Yet it’s still refreshing, despite being from last year, to read a story that focuses on the painstaking effort to trace scammers rather than lingering on the victim’s humiliation (looking at you, Netflix). Seal does explain how a French woman named Anne fell for “Brad Pitt” online and subsequently lost her fortune to the scammers, but her supposed savior, cyber‑detective Marwan Ouarab—sporting a cat‑in‑a‑trench‑coat T‑shirt—gets most of the page time here. Ouarab apparently found the scammers within 48 hours, but no charges have been made, and Anne is still fighting to recover any of her money. You can call the scam busters, but you’re still in for a long wait.

“All during the scam, Anne was suspecting something,” he says over a vanilla flan, a sweet treat for a very determined guy. “But every time, the crooks had fine words, the right words. They were really poetic. They knew what words were right for her. They really understood Anne’s psychological profile.”

It was a classic “sentimental scam,” says Ouarab—a carefully produced, all-encompassing “theatrical event” that uses love as the bait to hook the target and then envelops them completely in the con. (In this case, the divorced interior designer, Anne, whose last name has not been made public, and a convincing facsimile of Brad Pitt, achieved via A.I., deepfake technology, and, according to Ouarab, “ridiculous photoshop tools to create pictures of the fake Brad in his hospital bed.”)

More picks on scams

The Car-Crash Conspiracy

“High-speed accidents, crooked lawyers, and poor people desperate for cash—it was the kind of scheme that could have been cooked up only in the Big Easy.”

Joan Lowell and the Birth of the Modern Literary Fraud

“A century ago, an aspiring actress published a remarkable autobiography. She made up most of it.”

Meta’s Flirty AI Chatbot Invited a Retiree to New York. He Never Made It Home.

“A cognitively impaired New Jersey man grew infatuated with a Facebook Messenger chatbot with a young woman’s persona. His fatal attraction puts a spotlight on Meta’s AI guidelines, which have let chatbots make things up and engage in ‘sensual’ banter with children.”

My Scammer

“I responded to one of those spam texts from a “recruiter”—then took the job. It got weirder than I could have imagined.”

North Korea Stole Your Job

“For years, North Korea has been secretly placing young IT workers inside Western companies. With AI, their schemes are now more devious—and effective—than ever.”

title: Your Big Brain Wouldn’t Be Possible Without Sugar
content:
Humans have big brains, and those brains come with a big appetite for energy. The focus on what fueled the evolution of our massive noggins has centered on protein from meat, but a new analytical review published today in Science is reframing the story around a much sweeter center: glucose.

Featured Video

“While animal foods were important, the brain’s need for glucose has largely received little attention from anthropologists,” study author Jennie Brand-Miller said in a statement.

Nutritional scientists from the University of Sydney and University of Glasgow modeled dietary intake versus energy needs for varying brain and body sizes across 4 million years of hominin evolution. The models relied on data from the dietary composition of primates, fossil dental isotopes and morphology, genetics, and more. Over this 4-million-year period, brain size of hominins quintupled from 300 grams in Australopithecus afarensis to 1,500 grams in modern Homo sapiens, and metabolic needs increased accordingly.

Read more: “Why Is the Human Brain So Efficient?”

By calculating the “obligatory glucose demand” (the amount of energy required to run the brain, the body, and produce offspring) and comparing it to energy available from food sources, they determined simple carbohydrates played an outsized role in the development of outsized brains. According to the team, natural sugars from fruit, honey, and other sweet foods provided roughly 20 to 35 percent of energy intake throughout hominin evolution. After our ancestors tamed fire, they were able to unlock the complex carbohydrates in starchy foods, like tubers.

The study helps explain why we have such a sweet tooth, especially children whose brains can burn up to nearly two-thirds of the calories they consume. It also puts a new spin on the popular paleo diet. “The evidence suggests that carbohydrate-rich foods helped fuel the energy demands of our growing brains,” Brand-Miller said. “Rather than fearing carbohydrates, people should focus on high-quality sources, including whole fruits, legumes, and nutritious grains, and prioritize a range of carbohydrate foods as part of a healthy diet.” 

So go ahead and drizzle some honey on that steak—your inner hominin deserves it.

title: Dragon's Dogma 2 is getting a Fallout-inspired homesteading mod with fully customisable houses, and its creator has tons of big ideas for it
author: Fran Ruiz
content:
Cottagecore.

Dragon's Dogma 2: Dark Arisen is coming later this year, and before that, Capcom is releasing updates to address player complaints. But that doesn't mean modders are waiting for things to quiet down again before working on ambitious user-made expansions.

SonicaKP is a player who's been working on some interesting mods that seek to expand the open-world action RPG beyond its mechanical limits. Last month, they uploaded RiftSpeak to Nexus Mods, a PC modification that "gives your Dragon's Dogma 2 main pawn natural AI conversation and the will to act on it". Now, they're working on a familiar homesteading modification that seems to bring a lot of Fallout 4 & 76 into the world of Dragon's Dogma.

As seen in the gameplay demo shared above, the mod is still a work in progress, but the player can be seen building a house in the countryside from scratch after collecting some resources. It also shows plenty of pieces of furniture that can be acquired for the right amount of gold. While other customisation mods feel more like cheats and shortcuts to get cool stuff into the game, the vision behind this one seems more natural and adjusted to the vanilla game's rhythm and many systems.

SonicaKP isn't willing to share a tentative release date yet, but has teased it's part "of a much bigger expansion" that aims to include features like creature taming, new mounts (including griffins), actual homesteading mechanics, gardening, and more. Skyrim fans will think of the Hearthfire DLC as well, and I personally believe it was the main inspiration behind this mod.

Ahead of Dragon's Dogma 2: Dark Arisen's 9th October launch, we know Capcom and the game's core development team seek to "win back the trust" of RPG fans. Original DD1: Dark Arisen director Kenta Kinoshita has been tasked with leading the expansion-sized DLC, and he's confident he has "what it takes to continue the series' legacy".

title: The Legend of Zelda movie's Link, Benjamin Evan Ainsworth, couldn't play Breath of the Wild because of his age (and the lack of a Switch)
author: Fran Ruiz
content:
New generation.

The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom expanded the mainline series' horizons and brought in plenty of new players, but the actor playing live-action Link missed the former - initially due to his age.

While official marketing for the upcoming epic fantasy movie hasn't kicked off yet - it's targeting a 30th April, 2027, release date - Benjamin Evan Ainsworth is playing a fairly big role in House of the Dragon Season 3 as Daeron Targaryen. GamesRadar recently had a quick chat with the young actor, and of course, he was asked about how The Legend of Zelda is coming along.

While the 17-year-old couldn't say much, he revealed that he remembers when Breath of the Wild launched in 2017: "I remember being quite young at the time when it came out." But he "didn't have a Switch at the time", so he watched playthroughs instead. When Breath of the Wild was released, Ainsworth was only eight.

Still, it sounds like he eventually absorbed a proper dose of The Legend of Zelda history by "going back and realizing the 40 years of legacy and history, and the varied tones, the varied stories, the varied renditions and vocal performances of this character as well". No details on what he's done with Link yet, but he noted "it was an awesome thing to shoot".

Beyond Zelda and Link's casting - plus the fact production has taken place almost entirely in New Zealand - we don't know much about The Legend of Zelda. Wes Ball - of Kingdom of the Planet of the Apes and Maze Runner fame - is directing.

While the live-action movie won't arrive in time for the series' 40th anniversary, Nintendo has recently announced a remake of Ocarina of Time for Switch 2 coming in 2026, so our return to Hyrule is very near.

title: After dissolution of the original team, a Wuchang: Fallen Feathers sequel has been confirmed with the original creative director at the helm
author: Fran Ruiz
content:
Second wind.

Despite having over five million players since its launch last year and an okay enough reception, soulslike game Wuchang: Fallen Feathers quickly faced behind-the-scenes drama after its lead producer and director Xia Siyuan departed developer Leenzee, which crumbled later. It seems players will get a sequel after all, though.

Back in April, it was reported Digital Bros - the company that owns subsidiary 505 Games - had fully acquired the Wuchang IP for roughly €4m. Now, the publisher has confirmed via socials Xia Siyuan will be leading the development of a sequel to Wuchang with the new studio he founded after leaving Leenzee, Indolphinity (Chengdu Recursive Dolphin Technology).

505 Games will provide the funding and handle global publishing, and the sequel is now in the preparation phase. "Future development will remain firmly rooted in China," the announcement added.

Xia Siyuan also seems aware of the recurring criticisms of a mostly intriguing take on the soulslike genre that could grow with a sequel: "We listen closely to the real voices of players and the community, and we remain firmly devoted to our original creative aspirations and cultural foundations, striving to answer everyone's long‑standing expectations with more polished quality and a more complete experience."

Eurogamer's three-star review of Wuchang: Fallen Feathers called it "a competent, cool, and pretty soulslike with a nice twist on death, but few true surprises". On Steam, user reviews are currently 'very positive' if we look at the recent ones, with the overall rating limited to 'mostly positive', partially due to the performance and balance woes the game faced at first. It also launched on Xbox Series X/S (and on Game Pass day one) and PlayStation 5.

title: Double Fine hit with layoffs after exiting Xbox - "Only the survival of our studio would ever make us consider such a painful action"
author: Fran Ruiz
content:
"These actions are not taken lightly."

Nearly a month after it was announced Xbox was cutting 3200 jobs across the division and parting ways with four studios, Psychonauts 2 studio Double Fine Productions is laying off staffers to ensure its short-term survival.

On 28th July, studio head - and LucasArts veteran - Tim Schafer shared a brief announcement on social media revealing that 23 employees were being laid off. "Only the survival of our studio would ever make us consider such a painful action. Our transition to becoming an independent company also means becoming a size that we can sustain." According to Bloomberg reporter Jason Schreier, the studio was around 90 people before the cuts.

"We are committed to supporting each affected person as best as we can, and we thank them for their hard work and commitment to the creative spirit we cherish here at Doble Fine," the message by Schafer added.

According to Kotaku, an Xbox spokesperson shared the following statement: "Double Fine fully returned to independent management earlier this week, with their IP, catalog, and runway for their next games. As they begin their next chapter as an independent studio, we look forward to seeing what they create next." The studio's current runway is unclear. Shortly after exiting Xbox, Double Fine confirmed it would go back to being an independent studio and preserve its history and culture.

While at Xbox, Double Fine released Psychonauts 2, Keeper, and the multiplayer pottery game Kiln. As a high-profile studio known for off-beat games with a ton of heart, it's likely the team will be attempting to keep its spirit alive through similar projects, but this round of cuts will no doubt put more pressure on the remaining employees. Here's hoping there's a bright future ahead of the studio despite everything.

title: 30 Years Later, Quake Gets a Major Update With Loads of New Content
author: Tomas Franzese
content:
Follow

Link copied to clipboard

Published Aug 6, 2026, 5:55 PM EDT

Quake is still giving players new reasons to check the game out 30 years after launch

30 years later, Quake gets a major update with loads of new content

Sign in to your Polygon.com account

No new Quake game was announced to celebrate the franchise's 30th anniversary at this year's QuakeCon, but the beloved first-person shooter got a substantial update to mark the occasion. Developer MachineGames has released an entirely new Quake episode, and it's available across all versions of the game's 2021 remaster.

Titled Dawn of the Machine, the new episode comes from a studio best known for its work on the rebooted Wolfenstein games and 2023's Indiana Jones and the Great Circle. It previously worked alongside id Software and Nightdive Studios to make new episodes for the remaster, and did the same again for this 30th anniversary milestone.

Dawn of the Machine is built on the core of the 30-year-old game, but adds new enemy types and new weapons like the super axe and laser cannon. The 19-level episode is also designed to be replayed, as players can collect runes to unlock new paths on subsequent playthroughs and keep previously acquired health and ammo upgrades.

The update that adds Dawn of the Machine also adds a vault with behind-the-scenes assets from Quake's development, more achievements, and a cheats menu. On the multiplayer side of things, there's one new deathmatch map.

This Quake announcement comes at a moment when the future of id Software and MachineGames seems uncertain under Xbox. In particular, id Software was decimated by Xbox's July layoffs right after shipping DLC for Doom: The Dark Ages. It's unclear what id Software and MachineGames are making next as Xbox refocuses on its biggest franchises.

Dawn of the Machine is now part of the Nintendo Switch, PS4, PS5, Windows PC, Xbox One, and Xbox Series X versions of Quake.

title: Valve has released the CAD design files for the Steam Machine's exterior, leaving us asking: how long before someone makes a GabeCube skin?
author: Fran Ruiz
content:
Custom fit.

The Steam Machine has been among us for a few weeks now - albeit with a hefty price tag and limited availability - and knockoffs are already emerging. Meanwhile, Valve is letting users who are especially creative tinker with its exterior... if they can follow the instructions.

As explained by our friends at Digital Foundry, Valve has quietly released the CAD files for the Steam Machine's exterior under a "Creative Commons 'Attribution-NonCommercial-Sharealike 4.0 International' license, which allows sharing and adapting, but prohibits commercial work". It can be obtained here.

Valve's Pierre-Loup Griffais - one of the company's most publicly active engineers - noted that it's highly recommended that you let professionals do the work. "Any damage you do will not be covered by your warranty," he added. This is also part of the files' attached readme document.

These are technically meant to help users create custom front plates, but as always, Valve is expecting people to surprise them with bigger custom modifications. Just remember that any wrapper, skin, or front plate made with the help of these official files can't be sold legally.

In fact, you might remember renowned company dbrand - which focuses on accessories for electronic devices - had to bin its planned Companion Cube wrap in June, since it had somehow commenced work on and opened pre-orders for a Portal-inspired modification that hadn't been licensed from Valve. While it could return one way or another in the future, those original plans had to be scrapped for obvious reasons.

At the time of writing, I've yet to come across any designs made thanks to the official CAD files, but I'm holding out hope for a GabeCube design blending the classic Nintendo GameCube look - handle included, as DF's William Judd also said - and Valve iconography. Or maybe just make it a literal GabeCube.

title: Krafton have big plans for Subnautica, after the second game's once-divisive co-op "confirmed the potential to expand beyond the existing fan base"
author: Edwin Evans-Thirlwell
content:
Around half of players have never touched a Subnautica before, says exec

Subnautica 2 publishers Krafton may have had to pay Unknown Worlds a massive earn-out, after losing a farcical courtroom battle with ousted studio execs, but they're tickled pink by the ocean survival game's sales. According to Krafton's latest quarter-year financials, Subnautica 2 has sold over five million units since the early access launch.

They're now trumpeting its potential to become "our second franchise IP" after PUBG, in the words of head of investor relations Sophie Lee, which indicates that they're not only thinking about a possible Subnautica 3, but eyeing up Subnautica crossovers of all kinds. Think of the merchandising! Alterra lunchboxes! Reaper-branded cans of sardines! Nibbler Mango bodypillows! Maybe some kind of dastardly LLM-piloted luxury submarine!

Speaking to investors, Krafton's CEO Changhan Kim also noted that around half of the new game's players didn't play either the original Subnautica or Subnautica: Below Zero – an influx of fresh Subnauts Krafton attribute partly to the game having a co-op mode. Which is interesting, because Subnautica 2's co-op was controversial before release, with returning players worrying that it would steal focus and resources from the solo experience. Unknown Worlds seem to have put those fears to rest.

"On the new franchise IP front, the early performance of Subnautica 2’s early access launch confirms both our scale-up capabilities and its potential to become our second franchise IP," comments Lee, in Krafton's latest shareholder-flummoxing corpofusillade, as transcribed by Stock Analysis. "Subnautica 2 delivered a highly successful early access launch, both in the numbers and in how users responded." Even as they prioritise "community trust and game quality, maintaining stable service through to full launch", Krafton also plan to "scale up the Subnautica IP with a long-term perspective".

With Lee translating, CEO Kim added that "in particular, [Subnautica 2's] co-op content confirmed the potential to expand beyond the existing fan base to new user groups. This stems from our success in identifying an IP with a strong genre moat and scaling it up by expanding co-op and content volume while preserving the core gameplay of the original." I think that's "moat" as in "strong competitive advantage", though the more usual definition of a defensive ditch full of water sort of chimes with the subject matter.

I've enjoyed what I've played of Subnautica 2. It has excellently fishy energy. Though it does feel quite a lot like a retread of Subnautica 1. I can't say I'm gagging for it to become a massive entertainment property - I'm not really gagging for anything to become a massive entertainment property - but departed Unknown Worlds co-founder Charlie Cleveland does make movies nowadays. Perhaps there's scope for a collaboration, assuming he and Krafton can put all that "million dollar lawsuit" stuff behind them.

title: Rideshare "Stimulator" is an Uber driver sim set in a city full of weirdos that I'm hoping is satirical enough to pull the concept off
author: Oisin Kuhnke
content:
Pedal about halfway to the metal

Warhammer 40,000: Space Marine 2 developer Saber Interactive clearly like to keep themselves busy, as today they've announced the next game that they're publishing. It's called Rideshare "Stimulator" (I should note those quotation marks are a part of the title), and it is essentially a game all about being an Uber driver for a city full of oddballs.

Saber are no stranger to sim games, it's a big part of their bread and butter, and for the most part this is no different. As a rideshare driver, you need to pick up passengers and get them where they want to go, all while obeying the rules of the road, occasionally circumventing them if you're in a bit of a rush. How you drive and how well you look after your car is something your passengers will pick up on too, which might affect things like your rating, reviews and tips. You'll want those tips too, as you need to pay for all of your repairs and carwash trips yourself.

All of this, by and large, is generally what a real rideshare drive has to consider as well. The concept had me raise my guard a touch as I think gamifying labour that is notoriously exploited and underappreciated always feels a tad icky. But it does appear that developer Unigine are taking the satirical route here, as the passengers you pick up seem to lean towards the kind of person who you'd never want in your car.

One passenger may note how he's not banned from all aquariums, just the one, another may claim birds control the traffic lights, and others might compare you to their failure of a grandson. Whether this is remotely an accurate representation of your average Uber trip, I can't say, I can't even drive, but the silliness certainly seems to suggest that amongst the simulation aspect there is this quality of "man, this job can kinda suck." Though, that is a generous reading based on little information, so my guard is still up on this one.

I think all of this would read a tad better if it wasn't going for a photorealistic look, but I assume that wouldn't draw in the sim loving crowd. In any case, no release date attached to this one, so you'll have to keep your eyes peeled if it's of any interest.
